stories.extended_summary: At North Dakota State University's Central Grasslands Research Extension Center, researchers are testing virtual fencing—collars that create invisible boundaries for cattle. Graduate student Taleigh Adrian found that pastures with virtual fencing had more bee and butterfly species than those using season-long or patch-burn grazing. The cattle spend 50 days in a quarter of the pasture, then move to the next quarter, allowing the rest to recover. Over four years, each quadrant gets different treatments, and so far, cattle weight gain hasn't suffered. 'Utilizing virtual fencing technology is actually really beneficial for that pollinator community,' Adrian said, showing that technology can help both ranchers and nature.

stories.summary: The Wood County Fair's Ring of Dreams livestock show has doubled in size since 2023, now featuring 90 participants with developmental disabilities and 76 junior fair mentors. Creator Amanda Barndt keeps expanding the program with special touches, proving inclusion and community support can make a huge impact.
stories.extended_summary: In its fourth year, the Ring of Dreams show at the Wood County Fair has grown from 43 participants to 90, thanks to creator Amanda Barndt's relentless dedication. Participants with developmental disabilities get to show animals alongside junior fair mentors, with every detail from sign-up to show time designed to celebrate ability, not limitation. The Wood County Board of Developmental Disabilities and local sponsors back the event, which now includes Let Your Abilities Shine Day. This isn't just a livestock show—it's a movement of smiles, friendships, and real inclusion.
